title: Feedback on a water resources module

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Part 3. You will hear two environmental science students, Maya and Owen, talking to their tutor about their course. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26.

lines.speaker: TUTOR
lines.text: Thanks for coming in, both of you. As you know, we're reviewing the water resources module, so I'd like to hear what you thought of it. Shall we start with the lectures on water use?

lines.speaker: MAYA
lines.text: Sure. I found them really interesting, although some of it wasn't new to me. The number of people who still don't have safe drinking water, for example. That's been in the news so much.

lines.speaker: OWEN
lines.text: Yes, I knew about that too. But I was amazed by how much fresh water goes on farming. Around seventy per cent of all the water we take from rivers and from under the ground. I'd always assumed industry used most of it.

lines.speaker: MAYA
lines.text: Me too. I'd never have guessed it was that high.

lines.speaker: TUTOR
lines.text: And what about the session on leaks?

lines.speaker: MAYA
lines.text: Well, that's the thing. The lecturer only mentioned leaking pipes for a couple of minutes, and I'd have liked a lot more on it. It seems like such an obvious problem to fix.

lines.speaker: OWEN
lines.text: The bit that really surprised me was about clothes. Nearly three thousand litres of water to make one cotton T-shirt, mostly for growing the cotton. I had no idea.

lines.speaker: MAYA
lines.text: No, neither did I. I've been reading the labels on everything since then. The part about plastic bottles taking hundreds of years to break down was a bit obvious, though. We've all heard that a hundred times.

lines.speaker: TUTOR
lines.text: Fair point. Now, Owen, you went to the talk by the visiting speaker from the river trust, didn't you?

lines.speaker: OWEN
lines.text: Yes, about their project to monitor pollution in the local rivers. What I liked most was that the samples weren't collected by scientists. It was all done by local people who'd volunteered, and they were trained to do the tests themselves.

lines.speaker: MAYA
lines.text: I thought the drones were exciting, too.

lines.speaker: OWEN
lines.text: Well, they only tried those for a few weeks, and it didn't really work, so I wouldn't count that. But the other thing that impressed me was how long they'd been doing it. They've tested the same places every month for twelve years, so they can see real changes over time.

lines.speaker: MAYA
lines.text: And it was on the national news, which must have helped.

lines.speaker: OWEN
lines.text: Mm, I'm not so sure. I thought some of those reports made the rivers sound much worse than they really are.

lines.speaker: MAYA
lines.text: Well, at least the testing kits were cheap. I thought that was clever.

lines.speaker: OWEN
lines.text: Actually, the speaker said the kits cost far more than they'd expected. That was one of their biggest problems.

lines.speaker: TUTOR
lines.text: OK. And is there anything you think we should add to the module next year?

lines.speaker: MAYA
lines.text: I'd love a session on desalination, you know, taking the salt out of sea water.

lines.speaker: OWEN
lines.text: Really? I think that's more of an engineering topic. We'd spend the whole time on the chemistry. What I'd like is something on how water is shared between countries, when a big river flows through several of them.

lines.speaker: MAYA
lines.text: Oh yes, that's a great idea. There are so many disagreements about that around the world. I'd definitely support that.

lines.speaker: OWEN
lines.text: We've done plenty on climate change and rainfall already, so I wouldn't add any more of that.

lines.speaker: MAYA
lines.text: No. But what about water use in the technology industry? I read that data centres need huge amounts of water to keep their computers cool.

lines.speaker: OWEN
lines.text: Yes, I'd like that too. Most people have no idea about it.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.

lines.speaker: TUTOR
lines.text: Now, I'd like to hear about your project, the water-saving campaign you ran in the student halls. How did you go about it? First you had to choose a focus, didn't you?

lines.speaker: MAYA
lines.text: Yes. I wanted to focus on kitchens, because people leave the taps running while they wash up.

lines.speaker: OWEN
lines.text: And I was sure showers were the bigger problem. We actually had quite a heated argument about it, before we finally agreed on showers.

lines.speaker: TUTOR
lines.text: Then you did a survey of the residents.

lines.speaker: OWEN
lines.text: That's right. To be honest, a few people in our seminar group said surveys were a waste of time, but we never felt that. We wanted to know how long people really spent in the shower.

lines.speaker: MAYA
lines.text: And Dr Patel, who teaches the statistics course, gave us some really helpful advice on how to word the questions, so that people didn't just give the answers they thought we wanted.

lines.speaker: TUTOR
lines.text: Good. And then you designed the campaign itself.

lines.speaker: MAYA
lines.text: Our first idea was a set of posters. But the survey showed that most people had no idea how long they were in the shower. So we dropped the posters and gave everyone a small four-minute timer instead.

lines.speaker: OWEN
lines.text: That was a much better idea in the end.

lines.speaker: TUTOR
lines.text: And finally, the trial. How did that go?

lines.speaker: OWEN
lines.text: We thought it would be quite straightforward. We just had to read the water meters every day for two weeks.

lines.speaker: MAYA
lines.text: But it turned out to be much more difficult than we thought. Some of the meters were in locked rooms, so we kept having to ask the caretaker for keys, and a few readings were missed completely.

lines.speaker: OWEN
lines.text: We got there in the end, though, and we managed to show a real drop in water use.

lines.speaker: TUTOR
lines.text: Well done. That's an impressive result.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: That is the end of Part 3.

groups.stem: Which TWO facts from the lectures on water use were new information for Maya and Owen?

options.text: the number of people without safe drinking water
the share of fresh water used in agriculture
the amount of water lost from leaking pipes
the water needed to produce an item of clothing
the time it takes for plastic bottles to break down

groups.stem: Which TWO features of the river pollution project impressed Owen?

options.text: the use of members of the public to collect samples
the use of drones
the media attention it received
the low cost of the equipment
the long period over which data was collected

groups.stem: Which TWO topics do both students think should be added to the module?

options.text: removing salt from sea water
the effect of climate change on rainfall
the sharing of rivers between nations
the history of public water supply
water use in the technology sector

groups.instructions: Complete the flow-chart below. Choose FOUR answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–F, next to Questions 27–30.

evidence.quote: But I was amazed by how much fresh water goes on farming.

pairs: I was amazed … I'd always assumed industry used most of it
21.why: Owen is amazed that about seventy per cent of fresh water goes on farming, and Maya says she would never have guessed. So it was new to both. D is the other answer (see question 22).
21.trap: A was not new: Maya says it has been in the news a lot, and Owen knew about it too.

evidence.quote: Nearly three thousand litres of water to make one cotton T-shirt

pairs: I had no idea … No, neither did I
22.why: Owen had no idea how much water one T-shirt needs, and Maya says 'neither did I'. B is the other answer (see question 21).
22.trap: C (leaking pipes) was only mentioned briefly, and Maya wanted more on it. E (plastic bottles) was something they had 'all heard a hundred times'.

evidence.quote: It was all done by local people who'd volunteered

pairs: the samples weren't collected by scientists
23.why: What Owen liked most was that local volunteers, not scientists, collected the samples. E is the other answer (see question 24).
23.trap: B is wrong: Maya liked the drones, but Owen says the trial didn't work and he wouldn't count it.

evidence.quote: They've tested the same places every month for twelve years

pairs: the long period over which data was collected
how long they'd been doing it … every month for twelve years
24.why: The other thing that impressed Owen was that the project has tested the same places for twelve years. A is the other answer (see question 23).
24.trap: C is wrong: Owen thinks the news reports made the rivers sound worse than they are. D is wrong: the kits cost far more than expected.

evidence.quote: how water is shared between countries, when a big river flows through several of them

pairs: the sharing of rivers between nations
how water is shared between countries
25.why: Owen suggests how river water is shared between countries, and Maya says she would definitely support that. E is the other answer (see question 26).
25.trap: A (desalination) is Maya's idea, but Owen thinks it is more of an engineering topic, so they don't both recommend it.

evidence.quote: But what about water use in the technology industry?

26.why: Maya suggests water use in the technology industry, and Owen says 'I'd like that too'. C is the other answer (see question 25).
26.trap: B is wrong: they have already done plenty on climate change and rainfall. D (history) is never mentioned.

evidence.quote: We actually had quite a heated argument about it

27.why: Maya wanted kitchens and Owen wanted showers, and they argued before they agreed.

evidence.quote: gave us some really helpful advice on how to word the questions

pairs: Dr Patel, who teaches the statistics course, gave us some really helpful advice
28.why: Dr Patel teaches statistics, so he is a lecturer, and his advice on the survey questions was helpful.
28.trap: E is wrong: other students said surveys were a waste of time, but Owen says 'we never felt that'.

evidence.quote: So we dropped the posters and gave everyone a small four-minute timer instead.

pairs: Our first idea was … we dropped the posters … instead
29.why: Their first idea was posters, but after the survey they changed to shower timers.

evidence.quote: it turned out to be much more difficult than we thought

pairs: much more difficult than we thought
30.why: They thought reading the meters would be easy, but locked rooms and missed readings made the trial much more difficult.
30.trap: F is wrong: 'quite straightforward' was what they expected before the trial, not what happened.
